```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center",
  render = function(x, ...) {
    if (data.table::is.data.table(x) && !data.table::shouldPrint(x)) return(invisible(""))
    if (is.data.frame(x)) x <- knitr::kable(x, digits = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
    knitr::knit_print(x, ...)
  }
)
```

This tutorial runs a full spatial analysis on a public 10x Visium section of the
mouse brain: one anterior sagittal slice with 2,696 spots. You'll score LR
signaling between neighboring spots, map a signal onto the tissue, and trace it
back to the spots that sent it.

With `n.cores = 2`, the slowest step takes about 4 minutes.

## Get the data

`download_NICHESv2_data()` fetches the dataset from a NICHESv2 release on GitHub,
so you don't need any other package. The download is about 14 MB and happens
once; later calls read the saved copy.

```{r load}
library(NICHESv2)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

inputs <- download_NICHESv2_data("stxBrain", verbose = FALSE)
dim(inputs$count.mtx)
```

`inputs` holds the raw counts as a sparse genes x spots matrix, and the spot
metadata, which already has each spot's coordinates in `x` and `y`. To prepare
the same inputs from a Seurat object, see
[Starting from a Seurat object](seurat-objects.html).

## Choose a neighborhood

`Explore_Radius_Neighborhood()` shows how many neighbors each radius would give,
before you build anything.

```{r radius, fig.height = 3.6}
radius.table <- Explore_Radius_Neighborhood(
  inputs$meta.data[, c("x", "y")],
  r.max = 800
)
```

The curve rises in steps because Visium spots sit on a hexagonal grid. The first
step is the ring of 6 touching spots. This tutorial uses `k = 6`, which gives
those immediate neighbors. Passing `rad` instead would use a fixed radius.

This is one tissue section, so `sample.col` isn't needed. Set it when your data
has several sections, so that no edges cross between them.

## Build the NICHESObject

Raw counts give scores on an absolute scale. With `"connectomedb2025"` you don't
need to download anything else, and `species` must match your data.

```{r create}
obj <- create_NICHESObject(
  count.mtx = inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data = inputs$meta.data,
  LRM.db    = "connectomedb2025",
  species   = "mouse",
  mode      = "spatial",
  k         = 6L,
  method    = "product",
  n.cores   = 2L,
  verbose   = FALSE
)
dim(obj)
```

There's one row in `$edge.data` for each non-zero (edge, LR pair) score:

```{r edge-data}
nrow(obj$edge.data)
head(obj$edge.data, 3)
```

## Find the strongest signals

Summing across all edges shows which LR pairs dominate. Abundant genes rise to
the top, as they do with any magnitude-based score on raw counts.

```{r top}
obj$edge.data[, .(total.score = sum(score), edges = .N), by = LRM][
  order(-total.score)][1:5]
```

## Aggregate by neighborhood

```{r aggregate}
obj <- aggregate_NICHESObject(obj, verbose = FALSE)
agg <- obj$aggregations$neighborhood.edge.agg
```

This dataset has no cell-type labels, so we leave out `cell.type.col` and skip
the composition table.

## Map a signal onto the tissue

`Penk|Ogfr` is a useful example, because *Penk* is strongly enriched in the
striatum. `score.in.sum` adds up everything a spot receives from its neighbors
for this LR pair.

```{r map}
one.lrm <- agg[LRM == "Penk|Ogfr", .(cell, score.in.sum)]

plot.dt <- merge(
  obj$cell.meta[, .(cell, x, y)],
  one.lrm,
  by = "cell", all.x = TRUE
)
plot.dt[is.na(score.in.sum), score.in.sum := 0]

ggplot(plot.dt[order(score.in.sum)], aes(y, x, color = score.in.sum)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(NULL, labels = NULL) +
  scale_y_reverse(NULL, labels = NULL) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Received", trans = "sqrt") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Penk|Ogfr signal received per spot") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

## Trace a signal back to its senders

Because every edge is stored, you can see which neighbors sent the signal to the
strongest receiver. `share` is each sender's part of the total.

```{r trace}
receiver <- one.lrm[which.max(score.in.sum), cell]

senders <- merge(
  obj$edge.data[LRM == "Penk|Ogfr", .(edge, score)],
  obj$edge.list[ReceivingCell == receiver & SendingCell != receiver],
  by = "edge"
)
senders[, share := score / sum(score)]
senders[order(-score), .(SendingCell, score, share)]
```

```{r trace-plot, fig.height = 4}
spots  <- obj$cell.meta[, .(cell, x, y)]
center <- spots[cell == receiver]
nearby <- spots[abs(x - center$x) < 450 & abs(y - center$y) < 450]

arrows <- merge(senders, spots, by.x = "SendingCell", by.y = "cell")
arrows[, `:=`(x.end = x + 0.7 * (center$x - x),
              y.end = y + 0.7 * (center$y - y))]

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = nearby, aes(y, x), color = "grey85", size = 7) +
  geom_point(data = center, aes(y, x), color = "black", size = 7) +
  geom_segment(
    data = arrows,
    aes(x = y, y = x, xend = y.end, yend = x.end, linewidth = score),
    color = "#1f7a8c",
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(2.5, "mm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  scale_linewidth(range = c(0.4, 2), name = "Score") +
  scale_x_continuous(NULL, labels = NULL) +
  scale_y_reverse(NULL, labels = NULL) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Who sends Penk|Ogfr to the top receiver (black)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

All of these edges share one receiver, so the differences come only from how much
*Penk* each neighbor expresses. Two neighbors supply more than half of the signal.

## Export the edges

`export_to_TissuePlex()` needs the arrow package and writes one Parquet file.

```{r export}
out.file <- file.path(tempdir(), "edges.parquet")
export_to_TissuePlex(obj, output.path = out.file, celltype.col = NULL)
round(file.size(out.file) / 1e6)
```

The [export guide](tissueplex-export.html) shows what to do with that file.

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
unlink(out.file)
```

## Data source

The data are from 10x Genomics, "Mouse Brain Serial Section 1 (Sagittal-Anterior)",
Space Ranger 1.0.0, licensed under
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). NICHESv2 hosts a copy
taken from the `anterior1` object in the SeuratData package `stxBrain.SeuratData`.
The copy keeps the raw counts and spot metadata unchanged, and adds the spot
coordinates. The `PROVENANCE.md` file that comes with the download gives the
details.
